**I would prioritize a sharper Poisson analysis of the direct Gaussian Möbius target.** It looks most likely to produce a useful next theorem, while keeping the work connected to zero exclusion.

Its small-divisor deletion uses a coarse derivative estimate. The concrete next question is:

> Can we remove all divisors through \(D_k=e^{\alpha k}\), with an explicit \(\alpha>15\), while keeping the entire deletion error below \(\eta_N/16\)?

I would study the nonzero Poisson modes by stationary phase, tracking where their stationary points fall relative to the logarithmic Gaussian. A larger removable range would shrink the remaining cofactor range and make the signed arithmetic problem more focused. The improvement may be modest, so this should be a bounded investigation.

**The next step after that is the decisive one:** attempt a complete signed estimate for the retained Gaussian sum, with all block contributions and endpoints accounted for. The required bound is
\[
|\mathcal G_{k,t}|\le \eta_N/4
\]
uniformly over the prescribed samples and carrier interval. That would activate the existing zero-exclusion theorem.

My judgment is that the Poisson calculation has a better chance of yielding a rigorous near-term result; the signed estimate has the greater potential payoff. Neither centering nor sharper cutoffs alone supplies a new zero-free region. I would keep the new carrier-centered formula available as a tool for that signed estimate.
